sentences.text: Haplocheirus was a small coelurosaur and is classified as a dinosaur.
Gregory S. Paul estimated the animal was about 2 meters long and weighed 21 kilograms, while other measurements suggest a length of 1.9 to 2.3 meters and a weight up to 10.56 kilograms.

It differs from later alvarezsaurids by having heterodont dentition, featuring circular premaxillary teeth without serrations alongside flattened maxillary teeth with serrations along some of their length.
The skeleton retained the ancestral saurischian pubic bone orientation and possessed a notably robust first finger that was stronger than its second and third fingers.
The single known specimen, designated IVPP V15988, is preserved in near-perfect three-dimensional detail and includes the skull.
Histological examination revealed four lines of arrested growth, indicating the animal was approximately four years old at death.
This species is the most basal and oldest member of its group, predating others by approximately 63 million years and living about 15 million years before the first bird, Archaeopteryx.

The genus Haplocheirus was described by Choiniere and colleagues in 2010 from a fossil found in rocks dated between 161.2 and 158.7 million years old from the Shishugou Formation in the Junggar Basin of northwestern China.
The only known remains were discovered near the town of Wucaiwan in Xinjiang, China.
The slender teeth and lightweight skull suggest it primarily fed on small vertebrates.
Haplocheirus had long legs and was likely a fast runner.
Unlike most alvarezsaurs with highly modified forelimbs, this animal appears to have used its hands with proficiency comparable to other theropods of similar arm proportions.
Large eye orbits and wide scleral apertures suggest that Haplocheirus may have been adapted for nocturnal activity.
It possessed unusually long cochlear canals compared to other non-avian theropods, an adaptation likely linked to enhanced hearing capabilities.
The species name 'sollers' refers to the hypothetical behavior of using its three-fingered hands for activities other alvarezsauroids could not perform, such as capturing prey.
Some researchers hypothesize that the robust first finger was an adaptation for digging into tree trunks to access insects, similar to the modern aye-aye.

Haplocheirus is generally classified as an alvarezsauroid, identified as an alvarezsaur based on several unambiguous shared traits, and phylogenetic analyses identified it as the most basal member of the alvarezsauroidea group.
Haplocheirus lived during the Late Jurassic, between 161.2 and 158.7 million years ago, in the Oxfordian stage.
Dating of volcanic feldspar places the habitat of Haplocheirus at the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic.
The time range for Haplocheirus is from 161.5 to 154.8 million years ago.

Before Haplocheirus was found, there was a debate over whether alvarezsauroids were closely related to birds or if their similarities were due to convergent evolution, but Haplocheirus suggests that alvarezsaurid ancestry was conventional and not closely related to birds like dromaeosaurs or troodontids.

Some authors argue that Haplocheirus may be more closely related to ornithomimosaurs or that its classification as an alvarezsaur is not robust, while some analyses place it near ornithomimosaurs with support stronger than previous hypotheses linking it to avialae.
